propositions.text: Applicant is subject of removal order to Tunisia following negative PRRA decision on April 14, 2016.
propositions.quote: The applicant, Belhassen Trabelsi, is the subject of a removal order to be enforced on May 31 to return him to his country of citizenship, Tunisia. It follows an application for a pre-removal risk assessment (PRRA) which resulted in a negative decision on April 14, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant is subject to removal to Tunisia after a negative PRRA decision on April 14, 2016, says the court.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review of PRRA decision filed May 17 but not yet addressed.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review has not yet been addressed.

propositions.text: Stay application governed by three-part test from RJR-MacDonald and Toth: serious issue, irreparable harm, balance of convenience.
propositions.quote: The applicant must therefore satisfy the Court with regard to the three-part test set out in RJR-MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), [1994] 1 SCR 311; Toth v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 86 NR 302 (FCA).: 1. Is there a serious issue to be tried in the underlying judicial review? 2. Would the applicant suffer irreparable harm if removed from Canada? 3. Does the balance of convenience favour the applicant? Each component of the test must receive a positive response for the stay to be granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the stay application requires satisfying a three-part test and notes the judicial review application is pending.

propositions.text: Applicant cannot be found; counsel admits client cannot be contacted and affidavit not completed.
propositions.quote: By the very admission of counsel for the applicant, the applicant cannot be found. With commendable candor, this counsel submitted an affidavit in which he declared that [translation] “the client can no longer be contacted.” The client also failed to complete the affidavit in support of the application for a stay.

propositions.text: Respondent's counsel reports applicant did not appear for meeting with Canada Border Services Agency on May 24, 2016.
propositions.quote: After the hearing for the application for a stay, the Court was warned by counsel for the respondent that the applicant did not appear for the meeting set by the Canada Border Services Agency for the afternoon of May 24, 2016.

propositions.text: Other counsel representing applicant in other proceedings also indicates applicant cannot be found.
propositions.quote: Counsel other than that acting in this application for a stay but representing the applicant’s interest in other proceedings indicated that the applicant could not be found.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant cannot be found and failed to complete affidavit; respondent and other counsel confirm applicant's absence, says the court.

propositions.text: Application for stay requires person to appear with clean hands, good faith, and irreproachable attitude.
propositions.quote: An application for a stay requires the person to appear before the Court with clean hands, in good faith, and with an attitude beyond reproach.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that a stay application requires the applicant to appear with clean hands and good faith.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to act in good faith by not signing affidavit supporting stay application.
propositions.quote: I can only conclude that the applicant failed to act in good faith when he did not sign the affidavit in support of the grounds upon which a stay should be granted in his case.

propositions.text: Applicant's willingness to comply with removal order is unclear as he cannot be found and communicates only via Tunisian lawyer.
propositions.quote: In fact, it is not even clear whether he will submit to the removal order against him if it is not suspended, since he currently cannot be found and his only communication seems to be with a Tunisian lawyer.

propositions.text: Equitable remedies like stays may be denied if applicant does not come with clean hands.
propositions.quote: Brown and Evans, in their Judicial Review of Administrative Action in Canada (Carswell, loose-leaf), succinctly describe the nature of the Court’s power: Of course, being both discretionary and an equitable remedy, it may be denied where the applicant does not come to court with “clean hands”. [6:2130]

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant acted in bad faith by not signing affidavit and notes equitable remedies require clean hands.

propositions.text: Applicant must establish facts supporting stay application and attest to irreparable harm, especially for health reasons.
propositions.quote: Someone who wishes to benefit from an equitable remedy like a stay must at least establish the facts supporting the application. The applicant must attest to the irreparable harm, especially if health reasons are invoked.

propositions.text: Applicant's argument is eloquent but not founded on facts established by applicant; lack of evidence is problematic.
propositions.quote: Instead, we have an argument from counsel for the applicant, which is eloquent but is not founded on facts established by the applicant. This lack of evidence is clearly very problematic.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must prove facts and irreparable harm but failed to provide evidence, which is problematic.

propositions.text: Applicant's absence and lack of cooperation is troubling; only communication is with Tunisian lawyer.
propositions.quote: Also troubling is the applicant’s absence. His whereabouts are unknown, though he verbally communicated with a Tunisian lawyer to give a mandate to counsel now representing the applicant’s interests in his application for a stay.

propositions.text: Evidence and argument for irreparable harm are essentially non-existent due to applicant's non-cooperation.
propositions.quote: The scant evidence for irreparable harm and the argument based on that evidence are, so to speak, non-existent, as the applicant did not cooperate.

propositions.text: Applicant's attitude is far from irreproachable; courts should not reward those without clean hands.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s attitude is far from beyond reproach. Mr. Justice Nadon, of the Federal Court of Appeal, wrote in Baron v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), [2010] 2 FCR 311, 2009 FCA 81, at paragraph 65, that “neither enforcement officers nor the courts, for that matter, should encourage or reward persons who do not have ‘clean hands.’”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant's absence and lack of cooperation troubling and his attitude not irreproachable.

propositions.text: Applicant's failure to act in good faith suffices to dismiss stay application.
propositions.quote: In my mind, this suffices to dismiss the application for a stay.

propositions.text: No part of the three-part test for stay has been met after case review and hearing submissions.
propositions.quote: But there is more; after reviewing the case and hearing from counsel for the parties, I must conclude that no part of the three-part test has been met.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the stay application should be dismissed as no part of the three-part test is met.

propositions.text: Applicant was excluded under section 98 IRPA; PRRA assessed risks for first time.
propositions.quote: Since the applicant was excluded under section 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, chapter 27, the risks associated with his removal from Canada were assessed for the first time as part of the PRRA application.

propositions.text: PRRA decision was sophisticated and fair despite applicant presenting no arguments to decision-maker.
propositions.quote: The decision, which was very sophisticated and well-developed, was rendered without the applicant presenting any arguments to the administrative decision-maker.

propositions.text: Refugee Protection Division found serious grounds to believe applicant committed crimes in Tunisia, barring refugee status.
propositions.quote: the Refugee Protection Division found that there were serious grounds to believe that the applicant had committed crimes of common law in Tunisia corresponding to fraud, fraud on the government and money laundering. Mr. Trabelsi therefore cannot seek status as a refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Application for leave to seek judicial review of PRRA decision was denied under section 72 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The application for leave to seek judicial review was denied (section 72 of the Act).

propositions.text: PRRA decision involved pre-removal risk assessment as risk not assessed by Refugee Protection Division.
propositions.quote: Even though the applicant failed to present evidence or articulate an argument, the PRRA decision still involved a pre-removal risk assessment because the risk had not been assessed by the Refugee Protection Division.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the PRRA decision as fair and notes the applicant was excluded and denied refugee status due to criminality.

propositions.text: Stay application depends on judicial review leave; applicant must show serious issue to be tried.
propositions.quote: The application for a stay depends on the application for leave to seek judicial review from the PRRA decision. First, the applicant must satisfy this Court that there is a serious issue to be tried before the Federal Court if leave for judicial review is granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the stay application depends on judicial review leave and requires showing a serious issue to be tried.

propositions.text: Applicant bears burden of proof on balance of probabilities in PRRA and stay applications.
propositions.quote: The burden of proof falls on the applicant not only when making an application for a stay, but also before the PRRA decision-maker.

propositions.text: Cites Mandida and other cases confirming burden on applicant to prove risk on balance of probabilities in PRRA.
propositions.quote: Mr. Justice Mainville, when he was on this Court, wrote the following in Mandida v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 491 at paragraph 30: [30] In a pre-removal risk assessment, it is the applicant who bears the burden of proof. The standard of proof is the balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Evidence before PRRA decision-maker was painfully inadequate for unexplained reasons.
propositions.quote: For reasons that remain unexplained, the evidence before the PRRA decision-maker was painfully inadequate.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the applicant bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities but presented inadequate evidence to PRRA decision-maker.

propositions.text: PRRA decision-maker noted promised submissions were never received and investigated their absence.
propositions.quote: The PRRA decision-maker noted that the [translation] “submissions” promised when the applicant applied for a pre-removal risk assessment were never received. The decision-maker looked into whether they had, in fact, been sent. They had not.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA decision-maker found promised submissions were never sent and investigated their absence.

propositions.text: Only March 4 document related to applicant's medical situation was relevant; February documents were irrelevant.
propositions.quote: Of these three items, only the one from March 4 is useful for our purposes; those from February 8 and 26 are of no interest.

propositions.text: March 4 document alleged applicant's brothers lacked medical care in detention and applicant would face same.
propositions.quote: In this email, the applicants’ representative wrote: ‘You will note that two of our client’s brothers did not receive medical care while in preventive detention in Tunisia. We submit that this would be the case for Belhassen Trabelsi [the applicant] as well.’ These are the only allegations made by the applicant or the applicant’s representative in the context of this PRRA.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA decision-maker found only the March 4 document relevant, alleging applicant's brothers lacked medical care in detention.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to present positive evidence and sought to fault PRRA decision-maker's reasoning instead.
propositions.quote: Despite the burden of proof that lay on him, the applicant was content to oppose the PRRA decision-maker, who chose to examine the applicant’s situation based on the file as it was compiled, rather than rejecting the application due to lack of evidence or argument.

propositions.text: PRRA decision-maker articulated best possible argument with sparse evidence.
propositions.quote: The PRRA decision-maker, in fact, probably articulated the best possible argument that could be made with the sparse evidence in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant failed to present evidence and the PRRA decision-maker made the best argument possible with sparse evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant alleged deprivation of needed healthcare if returned to Tunisia.
propositions.quote: The applicant alleged that he would be deprived of the healthcare that he needs if he were returned to Tunisia (memorandum of fact and law, paragraph 18).

propositions.text: Cites Covarrubias case interpreting burden and standard for health-related risk under IRPA section 97.
propositions.quote: Below are three paragraphs taken from Covarrubias v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2007] 3 FCR 169, 2006 FCA 365, which address the paragraph of the Act that merits review in our case: ... These are also the paragraphs cited in the PRRA decision.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleged risk of healthcare deprivation; the court cites Covarrubias on burden and standard for health-related risk claims.

propositions.text: PRRA decision-maker found medical care needed for depression, cardiac issues, prostate nodule but Tunisia can provide it.
propositions.quote: Based on a very generous analysis of the conditions described in this judgment, the PRRA decision-maker found that medical care would be necessary for a depressive state, a cardiac situation, and a nodule discovered on the prostate, despite the fact that the medical evidence was scarce and lacking in description or details. In addition, Tunisia is able to provide the required treatment.

propositions.text: PRRA decision concluded applicant would not be deprived of medical care if returned and detained in Tunisia.
propositions.quote: I find that the applicant has not shown that, if he returns to Tunisia and is detained, he will not be able to receive the medical care normally available in Tunisia

propositions.text: Applicant tried to reverse burden of proof to require PRRA decision-maker to prove no risk, which is destined to fail.
propositions.quote: What was attempted through judicial review was to reverse the burden of proof, such that it would be up to the PRRA decision-maker to prove that there would not be a risk to the applicant’s life. This attempt is destined to fail.

paragraphs.summary: The PRRA decision found Tunisia can provide needed medical care; applicant's attempt to reverse burden of proof will fail, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to establish serious issue for judicial review due to lack of evidence and speculative arguments.
propositions.quote: There is no serious issue to be debated through judicial review of the PRRA decision, given the lack of evidence from the applicant, on whom the onus fell to demonstrate the evidence on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Applicant argued risk of unusual treatment not caused by inability of Tunisia to provide adequate care.
propositions.quote: If leave to seek judicial review is granted, the applicant must show the existence of a serious issue. However, he has in no way established the risk of unusual treatment, as argued by his counsel during the hearing for the application for a stay, where the risk of such unusual treatment is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care (subparagraph 97(a)(b)(iv) of the Act).

propositions.text: Applicant's argument about Tunisia's changes causing risk is pure speculation beyond balance of probabilities standard.
propositions.quote: As a result, there was a risk of not receiving treatment. This is pure speculation, far beyond the balance of probabilities standard (Li v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), [2004] 3 FCR 501; [2005] 3 FCR 239; Covarrubias cited above).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no serious issue for judicial review; applicant's risk argument is speculative and unsupported by evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant claimed PRRA decision-maker failed to review certain allegations not made in evidence.
propositions.quote: The applicant claimed that the case also included allegations other than those related to his medical condition. He reproached the PRRA decision-maker for not having reviewed allegations, which, according to the evidence, were never made.

propositions.text: Applicant's argument about unreviewed allegations is without merit.
propositions.quote: This argument is of no merit.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects applicant's claim that PRRA decision-maker failed to review unmade allegations as meritless.

propositions.text: Allegations were in unsigned, uncertified affidavit and submissions, so no affidavit or submissions exist.
propositions.quote: Those allegations were presented as an exhibit to the applicant’s affidavit, which he did not sign and which was not certified. There is therefore no affidavit and no proposed [translation] “submissions.” Furthermore, the [translation] “submissions” are also unsigned.

propositions.text: Merits of allegations considered and found without merit in PRRA context.
propositions.quote: I also considered the merits of these allegations. They are all without merit in the context of a PRRA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the allegations unsupported by signed affidavit and meritless in the PRRA context.

propositions.text: Applicant wrongly blames PRRA decision-maker for not considering implied submissions not made by applicant.
propositions.quote: I find it rather unusual to try to hold against the PRRA decision-maker the fact that he did not consider [translation] “implied submissions” regarding the applicant’s vulnerability, which, apparently, could have been found in the file.

propositions.text: Burden of proof lies with applicant to show need for protection under section 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: Here again, the applicant is behaving as though the burden of proof lay somewhere other than with him. He needed to satisfactorily show that he is a person in need of protection within the meaning of section 97 of the Act.

propositions.text: Applicant should complain about absence of submissions and evidence; blame lies with applicant alone.
propositions.quote: The applicant should be complaining about the absence of [translation] “submissions” and evidence. Therefore, the blame lies only with him.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant wrongly blames the PRRA decision-maker and bears sole responsibility for lack of evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant did not present arguments on irreparable harm, only on conviction in absentia and detention risk
propositions.quote: The applicant has not made any presentations in connection with irreparable harm. The comments presented were related to the fact that the applicant was convicted in absentia in Tunisia and that he will be detained on his return.

propositions.text: Irreparable harm is a distinct test requiring evidence and argument
propositions.quote: Irreparable harm constitutes a distinct test. The absence of evidence and arguments alone would have doomed it.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant did not present irreparable harm arguments, only conviction and detention risk; court states irreparable harm requires distinct evidence and argument.

propositions.text: Balance of convenience favors removal of people without status promptly under section 48 of the Act
propositions.quote: There is undeniable and substantial public interest in having people without status leave the country as soon as possible after a removal order becomes enforceable (section 48 of the Act).

propositions.text: Applicant filed stay application without confirming alleged facts and disappeared making counsel unable to find him
propositions.quote: In this case, the applicant has filed an application for a stay without confirming the alleged facts and, in addition, he has disappeared to the point where his counsel says he cannot be found.

propositions.text: Balance of convenience must favor the Minister given applicant's disappearance and unconfirmed facts
propositions.quote: Given the state of the case, the balance of convenience must favour the Minister.

propositions.text: Applicant leaving family in Canada does not favor him because he has disappeared
propositions.quote: Even the fact that the applicant is leaving his family in Canada cannot work in his favour because he has disappeared.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds balance of convenience favors Minister due to public interest and applicant's disappearance despite family ties; applicant filed stay without confirming facts.

propositions.text: Application for stay of removal order is dismissed
propositions.quote: Consequently, the application for stay of the removal order must be dismissed.

propositions.text: Order dismisses stay application to be enforced May 31, 2016
propositions.quote: ORDER THE COURT ORDERS that the application for stay of the removal order to be enforced on May 31, 2016 be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application for stay of removal order to be enforced May 31, 2016.
